take: Saudi Arabia's pipeline suspension threatens to remove 4% of global supply, with repairs potentially taking up to eight weeks, and Brent already above $108 whilst the Hormuz risk premium has opened a $40-plus gap between crude grades — this is the dominant bullish driver for both crude and products. South Korea's revival of long-haul crude import subsidies outside the Middle East adds further tonne-mile demand just as tanker rates hit seven figures for the first time and dry bulk effective capacity tightens on nearly 20% longer voyages and slower steaming. The inventory picture is jarringly at odds with the price action: API reported a 7.14 million barrel crude build for the week ending 11 September, even as Cushing stocks keep falling, so the headline build masks continued inland tightness. Watch the gasoil-bunker complex, where elevated crack spreads are already feeding through to pump prices whilst bunker markets digest both the crude spike and the financialisation of freight via SGX. In the next 24 hours, the EIA weekly petroleum status report will either confirm or contradict the API build, and any Saudi pipeline repair timeline update will set the tone for whether $108 holds.
